recognition: Recognize the public UCI Student Performance dataset (UCI 320), Portuguese-course records, and the Cortez and Silva 2008 study named in the supplied documentation. The dataset and its documented grade-prediction context are known; neither is claimed as new.
summary: I revise and retain I1 as a proposal for testing whether pre-G1 absence burden modifies the intention-to-treat effect of a structured tutoring offer made after G1. The supplied-data descriptive interaction is positive (0.678 grade points) but its 95% interval includes zero, and neither the absence window nor support timing is known. The search returned adjacent studies but no verified test of this moderator question. The randomized effect-modification claim remains untested and world-literature novelty is unestablished.

task.deliverable: Preserve the descriptive calculation as a feasibility check, then test a pre-registered student-level randomized tutoring offer after G1, stratified by a fixed pre-G1 absence measure.
acceptance: Interpret the current interaction only as conditional descriptive association: schoolsup is not a dated tutoring offer, absences have no specified observation window, and support was not randomized.

In the prospective protocol, record dated pre-G1 absence days, offer assignment, tutoring uptake and sessions, and dated G1 and G2 grades; compare assigned offer versus control within pre-specified absence strata under intention-to-treat.

Before enrollment, educators must set a practically useful interaction threshold and the analysis must be powered for it. Prioritize by attendance only if the pre-registered interaction estimate is positive and its confidence interval's lower bound exceeds that threshold; otherwise reject attendance-based prioritization while reporting any overall offer effect separately.
A literature comparison must distinguish abstracts from title-only records and must not claim exhaustive coverage or novelty from this single Crossref query.
task.proposed_computation: Completed on all 649 supplied rows: descriptive OLS of G2-G1 on schoolsup, absences >=3, their interaction, G1, failures, studytime, age and school, with HC3 uncertainty. No additional computation is requested.
task.proposed_search: Completed one Crossref search for secondary-school tutoring/support trials testing baseline absenteeism as a moderator of later grades. Its limited returned records do not settle prior-art coverage; no additional search is requested.

critique: The binary schoolsup field is reported extra educational support, not a dated offer of the structured tutoring intervention. Its association with grade change cannot estimate tutoring efficacy.
Absences are an undated total, so absences >=3 cannot be treated as a pre-G1 moderator in these records. The computation checks coding/overlap and a descriptive contrast only.
The adjusted grade-change interaction can be affected by regression-to-the-mean coupling because G1 is both part of G2-G1 and an adjustment variable. Treat it as exploratory, not causal.

For the trial, fix the eligibility and absence measurement window before randomization, randomize the offer within absence strata, date the grades, and record uptake and session dose. Pre-register a practically useful interaction threshold and power analysis.

final_idea.title: Does attendance burden modify the benefit of a post-G1 tutoring offer?
final_idea.question: Among secondary students eligible for support after the first grading period, does a randomized offer of structured subject tutoring improve second-period grade change more for students with higher absence counts measured strictly before G1 than for students with lower counts?
final_idea.new_claim: The proposed increment is a decision-specific effect-modification question: a dated pre-G1 attendance measure may help determine whether tutoring offers should be prioritized by attendance burden, beyond predicting grades. This is an untested hypothesis, not a finding.
final_idea.input_delta: Adds a defined post-G1 support decision, a temporally prior absence measure and a randomized-offer-by-absence contrast. The supplied material describes grade prediction and observational support but does not establish this intervention question.
final_idea.domain_value: Could guide whether schools should prioritize tutoring outreach for students with greater pre-period absence burden, if a randomized trial demonstrates a useful differential benefit.
known_basis_refs: input: official documentation defines G1 and G2 as first- and second-period grades on a 0-20 scale and schoolsup as extra educational support, without timing or assignment details
input: 649 student records from two Portuguese schools; absences are a count with no stated observation window
tool:c1: schoolsup-by-absences>=3 adjusted descriptive interaction 0.678 grade points, HC3 SE 0.486, normal 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631], N=649, design rank 9/9
assumptions: A prospective protocol can measure absence days strictly before G1 and record tutoring offer, uptake and dose.
Random assignment of the offer is ethical among eligible students; if not, a defensible randomized encouragement is required and the estimand must be changed accordingly.
G1 and G2 are dated and comparable 0-20 subject-grade measurements, with G2 recorded after the offer.
final_idea.variables_and_units: Student is the assignment and analysis unit. Record pre-G1 absence days over a fixed stated window (days), G1 and G2 grades (grade points, 0-20), randomized tutoring offer (0/1), uptake and attended sessions (sessions), school and subject. Primary outcome is G2-G1 in grade points. Pre-register a high-absence threshold with educators before enrollment; retain the continuous absence-by-offer interaction as a secondary analysis. The primary estimand is the difference between offer effects across the pre-specified absence strata under intention-to-treat.
final_idea.testable_prediction: The supplied-data proxy estimate is positive (0.678 grade points) in the predicted direction, but uncertain: its 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631] includes zero. This does not test the intervention claim. Proposal-only randomized prediction: the offer effect on G2-G1 is larger in the pre-specified high-absence stratum. No effect size is established.
final_idea.alternative: Absence burden may mark barriers that reduce tutoring uptake, so the offer effect could be smaller among students with higher absence counts; alternatively, schools may have targeted existing support to students with greater unmeasured need, distorting the observational proxy in either direction.
final_idea.discriminating_test: Run a pre-registered student-level randomized offer after G1, stratified by a threshold on absence days measured before G1. Compare assigned offer versus control on G2-G1 by stratum using intention-to-treat, and report the offer-by-absence interaction and interval. Record uptake to describe implementation without replacing the assignment estimand. Set a practically useful interaction threshold with school stakeholders before enrollment; support attendance-based prioritization only if the interval's lower bound exceeds that threshold. Otherwise reject that allocation rule, while estimating any overall offer effect separately.
final_idea.feasible_with_current_data: Only a descriptive proxy contrast is feasible. The supplied absences have no stated time window, schoolsup has no stated timing or dose, and support is not randomized. The randomized effect-modification question cannot be tested in these data.
final_idea.required_new_data: Prospective trial or randomized encouragement with student-level assignment; fixed-window timestamped absence days before G1; eligibility and randomization records; dated G1 and G2 subject grades; tutoring offer, uptake and session count; school and subject identifiers; and a stakeholder-defined minimum useful interaction threshold with an adequate power calculation.
final_idea.failure_condition: For the proposal, the allocation hypothesis fails if a sufficiently powered pre-registered trial does not show a positive offer-by-absence interaction whose confidence interval lower bound exceeds the predeclared useful-benefit threshold. A null or negative result rejects attendance-based prioritization, though it does not by itself rule out an overall tutoring benefit.
final_idea.nearest_prior_query: Search randomized or encouragement-based secondary-school tutoring studies that test baseline absenteeism as a moderator of subsequent grade effects, distinguishing such moderation from observational support allocation and grade prediction.

final.what_changed: The original question is retained but tightened: the absence window must end before G1, the follow-up is a randomized offer after G1, and an educator-defined practical interaction threshold is required for the allocation decision. The unadjusted hypothesis remains proposal-only; the computed quantity is only a descriptive association using proxies.
final.what_is_known: The executed calculation used 649 rows. Cell counts were absences <3/support no=322, absences <3/support yes=44, absences >=3/support no=259, and absences >=3/support yes=24. The adjusted interaction was 0.678 grade points, HC3 SE 0.486, normal-approximation 95% interval [-0.275, 1.631], with full design rank 9/9. The estimate is directionally consistent with the frozen descriptive prediction but does not distinguish it from zero at this interval level. Timing and confounding prevent a causal interpretation.
final.what_is_new_hypothesis: Relative to the supplied prediction-focused documentation, the added hypothesis is that pre-G1 absence burden modifies the causal effect of a post-G1 tutoring offer on G2-G1 and could support a targeted allocation rule. The supplied data and search results do not establish this hypothesis or its novelty in world literature.
final.falsifier: A sufficiently powered randomized trial in which the pre-registered offer-by-absence interaction's interval does not exceed the stakeholder-defined minimum useful benefit falsifies the proposed attendance-based prioritization rule. A sufficiently precise non-positive interaction is especially contrary to the directional prediction.
final.minimum_next_test: Specify a fixed pre-G1 attendance window and eligibility rule; obtain educator agreement on the minimum useful interaction; calculate trial power; then randomize the tutoring offer within absence strata and measure dated G1, offer/uptake, and G2. Report intention-to-treat stratum effects and the interaction with uncertainty.

final.nearest_work_comparison: The returned abstract for s1_S1 concerns non-random sorting into Islamic secondary schools and achievement, not tutoring or attendance moderation. The abstract for s1_S6 describes a small attendance-monitoring intervention for absenteeism, not a tutoring effect on grades or an attendance moderator. s1_S2 and s1_S3 are titled Taabo Tutoring Study but have title/date/DOI only; their population, design, outcomes and moderator cannot be inferred. Other results are title-only or unrelated to the target relation. This search did not verify an exact prior test, but its stated limited coverage cannot establish absence of prior work.
final.novelty_status: Input-relative increment: explicit randomized post-G1 tutoring-offer effect modification by pre-G1 absences tied to an allocation decision. World-literature novelty is unverified; the single limited Crossref result set is insufficient for a novelty claim.
final.limitations: The supplied dataset is observational, limited to two Portuguese schools and 649 records, and its absence timing and support timing/dose are unspecified. The 24 high-absence/support-yes records and 44 low-absence/support-yes records are modest cells. The grade-change interaction uses G1 both in the outcome difference and as an adjustment covariate, so regression-to-the-mean coupling is possible. HC3 uncertainty does not address unmeasured confounding, selection, measurement error or clustering. The computed result is not randomized-trial evidence. The literature search is relevance-ordered and incomplete; title-only records support no finding-level comparison.
